## Methods

Reagents and primary antibodies
Sodium butyrate and β-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA) and dissolved in Ultra PureTM water (Invitrogen, Waltham, MA, USA) in stock solutions. Stock solutions of butyrate and BHB were filtered through a 0.2 µm membrane and stored at -80 °C. Working solutions were freshly prepared by diluting the stock solutions with UltraPureTM water. Trichostatin A was purchased from Sigma and dissolved in DMSO. All chemicals were obtained from Sigma unless stated otherwise.
Antibodies against Histone 3 (Cat.no.4499), AcH3K9 (Cat.no.9649), AcH3K18 (Cat.no.13998), AcH3K27 (Cat.no.8173), STAT3 (Cat.no.9139), phosphorylated-STAT3 (Cat.no.9145), and a kit of HDACs antibodies (Cat.no.9928) were purchased from Cell Signaling Technologies (Danvers, MA, USA). Antibodies against Histone 4 (Cat.no.ab177840), AcH4K5 (Cat.no.ab519987) and AcH4K12 (Cat.no.ab177793) were obtained from Abcam (Cambridge, UK). Antibodies against Adenylyl cyclase III (Cat.no.sc-588) and GAPDH (Cat.no.sc-32233) were purchased from Santa Cruz Biotechnology (Dallas, TX, USA). Acetylated-α-tubulin (Cat.no.T7451) antibody was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA).

Cell culture
The hypothalamic N38 cell line was purchased from Cedarlane (Ontario, Canada) and cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (P/S). For butyrate treatment, cells were incubated with butyrate at 0.01 to 20 mM final concentration for 24 hours period before harvested unless stated otherwise. All of cell culture experiments were performed in biological triplicate unless stated otherwise.

Animal
The Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at the Avison Biomedical Research Center, Yonsei University, approved all animal protocols utilized in this research (Approval No. 2022-0056). All experiments were performed using inbred C57BL/6J mice. To generate hypothalamic primary cilia knockout mice, mice carrying the Ift88 floxed allele (Jackson Laboratory, Strain no.022409) were crossed with either AgRP-ires-cre (Jackson Laboratory, Strain no.012899) or SF-1-cre (Jackson Laboratory, Strain no.012462) mice. Whenever stated, mice were backcrossed with the Cre-dependent reporter Gt(ROSA)26Sor (Ai9) mouse line (Jackson Laboratory, B6;129S6-Gt(ROSA)26Sortm9(CAG-tdTomato)Hze/J, Strain no.007905) to identify cells with Cre recombinase activity using td-Tomato fluorescence. For comparisons of primary cilia length between hypothalamic AgRP/NPY and POMC neurons, heterozygous transgenic mice expressing humanized Renilla green fluorescent protein (hrGFP) under the control of the Npy (Jackson Laboratory, Strain no.006417) or Pomc1 promoter (Jackson Laboratory, Strain no.006421) were used. Both male and female mice were included in metabolic phenotyping experiments, whereas male mice were used for molecular, histological, and electrophysiological analyses. Mice were housed in individual cages under the specific pathogen-free condition, with a 12:12 h light:dark cycle (light automatically on/off at 08:00-20:00) at 22±1 °C and with 55% humidity. Mice were fed either a high fat diet (HFD, Research Diets, 60% calories from fat, Cat.no.D12492) or control chow diet (PicoLab® Rodent diet 20, LabDiet, 13.2% calories from fat) and provided with distilled water ad libitum.
For experiments with peripheral butyrate administration, 8- to 10-week-old male mice were stabilized on HFD feeding for 7 days before starting butyrate treatment. pH-matched (7.45±0.03) solutions of sodium butyrate (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Cat.no.sc-202341C) and sodium bicarbonate buffer as the control were prepared at final concentration of 100 mM and provided ad libitum via the drinking water bottles. Butyrate and control solutions in drinking bottles were freshly replaced every 3 days. For experiments with i.p. butyrate administration, sodium butyrate (500 mg/kg of body weight) and sterile control saline were injected i.p. daily after measuring the body weight.
For experiments with ICV injection, mice after full recovery from ICV cannulation were stabilized on HFD feeding for 7 days before starting ICV injection treatment. 2.5 µL of 1.25 µg/µL sodium butyrate solution or control saline were daily infused via inserted ICV cannula into the third ventricle at an infusion rate of 2.5 µL/min using the microinjection syringe pump (LEGATO® 100 syringe pump, KD Scientific, MA, USA). Body weight was monitored daily before injection. At the end of experiments, mice were perfused using 10% neutral-buffered formalin solution or euthanized by decapitation. Blood plasma and tissues samples were snap frozen in dry ice and stored at -80 °C before analyzed. Perfused organs were kept at 4 °C in the 10% neutral-buffered formalin solution.

ICV cannulation and injection procedure
Male and female mice (10-12 weeks old) were anesthetized with an i.p. injection of Zoletil and Rompun (30 and 7.5 mg/kg, respectively) and mounted on a stereotaxic frame (KOPF1900, David Kopf Instruments, CA, USA) under aseptic conditions. Guided by the Paxinos and Franklin mouse brain atlas, a 26-gauge stainless steel guide cannula was stereotaxically implanted into the third ventricle (coordinates from bregma: AP −1.8 mm, DV −5.0 mm) and secured to the skull with dental cement. Post-surgery, the animals received a single i.p. injection of ketoprofen (5 mg/kg) for analgesia and were individually housed for at least a 7-day recovery period. To verify functional cannula placement, mice were centrally infused with angiotensin II (50 ng in 2.5 µL, rate of 2.5 µL/min). Only those exhibiting a robust dipsogenic response within 5 minutes were included in subsequent experiments; non-responders were excluded. Prior to the actual ICV treatments, all mice underwent three days of habituation to handling and restraint to minimize stress. Finally, the anatomical accuracy of the cannula placements was confirmed post-mortem.

Stereotaxic virus injection
Eight-week-old male mice were anesthetized via an intraperitoneal injection of a Zoletil and Rompun cocktail (30 and 7.5 mg/kg, respectively). Under aseptic conditions, the skull was exposed via a minor incision and drilled at the designated coordinates. We stereotaxically injected 500 nL of either AAV2-Cre-GFP (Addgene, Cat. No. 105545) or AAV2-GFP (Addgene, Cat. No. 105530) into the third ventricle (3V) of the hypothalamus (AP: −1.76 mm, ML: 0 mm, DV: −5.25 mm relative to bregma). The viral vectors were delivered at a constant rate of 50 nL/min over 10 minutes, with the injection needle left in situ for another 5 minutes to prevent backflow. Post-operatively, animals recovered on a heating pad to maintain body temperature. A minimum three-week period was provided to ensure complete surgical recovery and adequate Cre expression prior to experimental interventions. Finally, accurate viral targeting in the 3V was confirmed post-mortem using immunohistochemistry (IHC); animals with off-target injections were excluded from the final analysis.

Food intake measurement
Daily food consumption was calculated by subtracting the weight of the remaining chow from the initial amount provided every 24 hours. We monitored this intake for the first 5 days following the onset of treatment and utilized the average daily consumption for our comparative analyses. To ensure data accuracy, measurements from mice exhibiting food-crumbling behavior were excluded from the final analysis.

Glucose and insulin tolerance tests
Following 3 to 4 weeks of butyrate administration, we conducted glucose and insulin tolerance tests (GTT and ITT). Prior to testing, mice were fasted overnight for the GTT or for 2 hours for the ITT, while maintaining free access to water. Mice were i.p. injected with a solution of D-glucose (1.5 g/kg of body weight) or insulin (1.2 U/kg of body weight; HumulinR, Elli&Lilly) prepared in saline for GTTs and ITTs, respectively. Baseline (t0) and post-injection blood glucose levels were recorded at predetermined intervals by sampling tail-vein blood using a ContourTS hand-held glucometer (Bayer, Germany).

Metabolic cage study
To evaluate indirect calorimetry, HFD-fed mice receiving either butyrate or a vehicle control were placed in a 12-channel PhenoMaster Home Cage System (TSE Systems Inc.) featuring triple-beam infrared technology. The animals were single-housed and allowed to acclimatize to the metabolic chambers for 48 hours under standard experimental conditions. Following this habituation, we continuously monitored various metabolic indices—including oxygen consumption (VO2), carbon dioxide production (VCO2), energy expenditure, locomotor activity, and ingestive behaviors (food and water intake)—over a 5-day period. Throughout the evaluation, mice had ad libitum access to chow and water.

Measurement of body composition (Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry)
For the analysis of body composition, the fat and lean masses of the mice were quantified using a dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scanner (InAlyzer™, MEDIKORS, Korea) under brief isoflurane anesthesia. Following calibration according to the manufacturer's instructions, the system's lower limit of detection was established at 0.001 g/cm².

Measurements of metabolic hormones
Blood samples obtained via tail-nick were collected into EDTA-treated capillary tubes (Microvette CB300, Sarstedt). Following centrifugation to isolate the plasma, the aliquots were immediately frozen and maintained at −80 °C. The circulating concentrations of insulin and leptin were subsequently quantified using commercial ELISA kits (Morinaga Institute of Biological Science, Yokohama, Japan) in strict accordance with the manufacturer's provided protocols.

Immunoblotting
Cells or tissue homogenates were washed in 1X PBS and subsequently lysed using RIPA buffer (containing 150 mM NaCl, 50 mM Tris pH 8.0, 1% Triton X-100, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, and 0.1% SDS) enriched with phosphatase and protease inhibitor cocktails (Roche, Basel, Switzerland). Total protein concentration was determined via the Bio-Rad Protein Assay system (Bio-Rad Laboratories, CA, USA). Equivalent quantities of protein lysates were resolved by SDS-PAGE on acrylamide gels and electro transferred to nitrocellulose membranes. For blocking, the membranes were treated with 5% non-fat milk in TBST (Tris-buffered saline containing 0.1% Tween 20) before an overnight incubation at 4 °C with the respective primary antibodies under gentle agitation. After washing the membranes four times in TBST, they were exposed to species-appropriate secondary antibodies for 1 hour at room temperature on a shaker. Following an additional four washes with TBST, the protein bands were developed using an ECL substrate and captured on X-ray film or a chemiluminescence imaging platform.

Quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR)
Total RNA was isolated from cultured cells or tissue homogenates utilizing the Trizol reagent (Life Technologies, CA, USA). Following RNA quantification via a NanoDrop spectrophotometer, 0.5 to 1 µg of the purified RNA was converted into cDNA with the ReverTra Ace-α-™ synthesis kit (Toyobo, Osaka, Japan). The qPCR was subsequently performed on a CFX Connect Real-Time System (Bio-Rad, CA, USA). Each reaction mixture contained 1 µL of the cDNA template, target-specific primers, and iQ SYBR Green Supermix. To ensure accurate quantification, all gene expression data were normalized to 18S ribosomal RNA (18S) as the endogenous control.
Primer sequences used in qPCR were as follows: 18S: F, 5′-AACCCGTTGAACCCCATT-3′, R, 5′-CCATCCAATCGGTAGTAGCG-3′; Agrp: F, 5′-CGGCCACGAACCTCTGTAG-3′, R, 5′-CTCATCCCCTGCCTTTGC-3′; Foxj1: F, 5′-CCCTGACGACGTGGACTATG-3′, R, 5′- GCCGACAGAGTGATCTTGGT-3′; Ift20: F, 5′-AGGCAGGGCTGCATTTTGAT-3′, R, 5′- CAAGCTCAATTAGACCACCAACA-3′; Ift27: F, 5′- GGGACCCATTTCCAGAAGAA-3′, R, 5′- CCGGCTGAGTCAAAAATGAA-3′; Ift54: F, 5′- TGTGTAAGAGTGCGCTTCCC-3′, R, 5′- GCATGCTGCCTGTTCTCACT-3′; Ift88: F, 5′- GCAGTGACAGTGGCCAGAAC-3′, R, 5′- AAGGTTGCATCTGTCCCAGGC-3′; Kif3a: F, 5′- AGCTGCGATAATGTGAAGGTG-3′, R, 5′- GTTCCCCTCATTTCATCCACG-3′; Kif3b: F, 5′- GGACTGTGTGTGGAGCCTTG-3′, R, 5′- CTGACAGAGGCAGGCACCTA-3′; Npy: F, 5′-CTACTCCGCTCTGCGACACT -3′, R, 5′-AGTGTCTCAGGGCTGGATCTC-3′; Pomc: F, 5′-CAGGTCCTGGAGTCCGAC-3′, R, 5′-CATGAAGCCACCGTAACG-3′; Rfx1: F, 5′- GGCAGCCAGAAGCAGTATGT-3′, R, 5′- GCACCTTCCGATACGGTGA-3′; Rfx2: F, 5′- TGTGAGCCGATCCTACAGTG-3′, R, 5′- CCGCAGCACATCTGGGATAAG-3′; Rfx3: F, 5′- AGCTCGGGAGGAACCTATTTG-3′, R, 5′- GACAGACCGTCAGACTTTTGC-3′; and Rfx4: F, 5′- GACAGCTTAACTCAGGTGATCC-3′, R, 5′- GTTTTCCGGGAGATCGTGGAG-3′.

Immunofluorescence (IF) staining and quantification of cilia length
Cells grown on coverslips were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) for 10 minutes at room temperature, followed by an overnight incubation at 4 °C with an anti-acetylated-α-tubulin antibody under gentle agitation. For brain tissue analysis, mice underwent transcardial perfusion with 10% neutral-buffered formalin (Sigma-Aldrich, MO, USA). Extracted whole brains were cryoprotected overnight in a 20% sucrose/PBS solution and subsequently sliced into 25-µm sections utilizing a Leica CM1850 cryostat (Wetzlar, Germany). Fixed cells or brain sections were blocked in 3% goat serum prepared in 1X PBS with 0.25% Triton® X-100 (0.25% PBST) for 1 hour and incubated with the acetylated-α-tubulin antibody (for staining primary cilia in cells) or the adenylyl cyclase III antibody (for staining primary cilia in brain sections) prepared in PBST for 24 hours at 4 °C on a shaker. After washing 4 times with 1X PBS, cells or brain sections were incubated with the Alexa Fluor 488 secondary antibody (Invitrogen, CA, USA) prepared in 0.1% PBST. After washing 4 times (10 min for each) with 1X PBS, cover glasses of stained cells and brain sections were mounted using the Fluoroshield Mounting Medium with DAPI (Abcam, Cat.no.ab188804) and visualized with the Zeiss LSM700 Confocal Laser Scanning Microscope. Captured images generated from the ZEN 3.0 SR software of the microscope system were subjected to the ImageJ CiliaQ Plugins software tool (https://github.com/hansenjn/ CiliaQ) for an automated quantification of ciliary length57 or analyzed by an independent researcher without prior knowledge of experiment identity.

Histological analysis
White adipose tissues collected in 10% neutral-buffered formalin solution were paraffin embedded, sectioned and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) following a standard protocol. Stained samples were visualized and captured by the Leica ICC50E microscope system (Leica Microsystems, Wetzlar, Germany). Captured images were subjected to the ImageJ Adiposoft Plugin software tool (https://imagej.net/plugins/adiposoft) for an automated quantification of adipocyte and lipid droplet size58.

Brain slice preparation and electrophysiology
Five to seven-weeks-old male WT (AgRP-cre;tdTomatoF/+) or IFT88 KOAgRP (AgRP-cre;IFT88F/F;tdTomatoF/+) mice carrying a Cre-dependent tdTomato reporter allele were used for electrophysiological experiments. For slice preparation, mice were decapitated, and their dissected brains were quickly immersed in ice-cold, oxygenated cutting solution containing (in mM): 208 Sucrose, 2.5 KCl, 0.5 CaCl2, 6 MgCl2, 11 D-glucose, 1.4 NaH2PO4, 25 NaHCO3, and 0.5 sodium ascorbate. Coronal hypothalamic slices (300 µm thick) were prepared using a vibratome (7000SMZ-2, Campden Instruments, Loughborough, England). The slices were then incubated at 30 °C for 1 hour in oxygenated artificial cerebrospinal fluid (ACSF) with composition (in mM): 126 NaCl, 2.5 KCl, 2.4 CaCl2, 1.2 MgCl2, 11 D-glucose, 1.4 NaH2PO4, 25 NaHCO3 and 0.5 sodium ascorbate (osmolarity 310–320 mOsm, pH 7.3-7.4, bubbled with 95% O₂/5% CO₂).
For recordings, slices were transferred to a recording chamber perfused with oxygenated ACSF at a flow rate of approximately 2 mL/min using a gravity-driven perfusion system. AgRP-expressing neurons in the arcuate nucleus (ARC) were identified via brief epifluorescence exposure on a Nikon FN1 upright microscope (Nikon Instruments Inc., Melville, NY, USA) equipped with a 10× water-immersion objective and differential interference contrast optics. Whole-cell signals were amplified using a Multiclamp 700B amplifier (Molecular Devices), filtered at 2 kHz, and digitized at 10 kHz using a Digidata 1440A interface (Molecular Devices). Recording pipettes, fabricated from borosilicate glass using a Flaming-Brown puller (P-1000, Sutter Instruments), had a tip resistance of 3–5 MΩ. The standard pipette solution contained (in mM): 130 K-gluconate, 10 KCl, 1 CaCl2, 1 MgCl2, 10 HEPES, 4 MgATP, and 10 EGTA, with the pH adjusted to 7.3 using KOH, for current clamp data and spontaneous excitatory post-synaptic currents (sEPSCs) under voltage clamp mode at -70 mV. sEPSCs were recorded in the presence of 100 µM picrotoxin (PTX) in ACSF. For recording spontaneous inhibitory post-synaptic currents (sIPSCs), ACSF containing 10 µM 6-cyano-7-nitroquinoxaline-2,3-dione (CNQX) and 50 µM D-2-amino-5-phosphonopentanoic acid (DL-AP5) was used, along with a high-Cl⁻ intracellular pipette solution (130 mM KCl replacing K-gluconate). Under the high [Cl⁻], the reversal potential for Cl⁻ was 0 mV, resulting in inward GABA-mediated currents at -70 mV. All recordings were performed at room temperature using pCLAMP 10.7 software (Molecular Devices). Resting membrane potential (RMP) and action potential (AP) firing properties were assessed after 5 minutes of whole-cell configuration. Series resistance (Rs) was monitored at the beginning and end of each experiment, and data were discarded if neurons exhibited Rs greater than 20 MΩ or if it changed by more than 20% during the recording. CA neuron was classified as depolarized or hyperpolarized if its RMP shifted by at least 2 mV. Membrane potentials were not corrected for liquid junction potential (-8 mV). AP firing frequency, as well as synaptic current frequency and amplitude, were analyzed using Mini Analysis software (ver. 6.0.7; Synaptosoft Inc., Decatur, GA, USA).

Statistics
Statistical significance was determined using Student’s t-test, chi-square test, and two-way ANOVA, as appropriate, using GraphPad Prism 8.0 software (GraphPad Software, Inc., CA, USA). Detailed statistical test(s) used and corresponding p-value are described in figure legends. For all analyses, p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The current manuscript investigates the role of neuronal primary cilia in the central effects of butyrate. The study demonstrates the impact of butyrate on energy metabolism and identifies AgRP cilia as key mediators of its effects. The authors first show that chronic central administration of butyrate protects against diet-induced obesity, which correlates with increased primary cilia length in hypothalamic neurons. Interestingly, by knocking down IFT88 in SF-1 or AgRP neurons, the authors demonstrate that butyrate acts specifically on AgRP neurons to modulate metabolism.

The present study is clear and well-written; the objectives are well-defined, and the experiments are thoughtfully designed and executed in an elegant manner. The discussion is well-supported by the results.

While the overall quality of the manuscript is exceptional, I find a few points that need to be addressed:

Major Comments:
-Are the effects of butyrate only observed during high-fat diet (HFD) exposure? All the presented results are from diet-induced obese mice. Does butyrate affect energy metabolism in mice maintained on a chow diet?
-A considerable amount of work is conducted using the N38 cell line. While this is acceptable, it is evident that this cell line expresses various HDACs at higher levels than those found in the hypothalamus. In this regard, are cilia-related genes regulated in the hypothalamus of mice treated with butyrate?
-Are female mice also affected by butyrate? Including data or a brief discussion on potential sex differences would strengthen the manuscript.
-The authors report changes in primary cilia length in ARC neurons. Since they show that primary cilia in AgRP neurons are critical for the metabolic effects of butyrate, would it be possible to quantify the primary cilia length specifically in AgRP neurons? Is there any difference in cilia morphology or length between AgRP and POMC neurons?

### Reviewer 2

Rijal et al.'s work investigates the neuronal and molecular substrates that mediate the behavioral (primarily eating) and metabolic effects of butyrate. The main findings, as stated in the discussion, are that the cilia of Agrp-expressing neurons are required for butyrate-mediated effects and that central administration of butyrate produces effects similar to those reported following peripheral administration. While primarily of interest to a very specialized audience, these results might be relevant to the broader audience interested in the mechanisms controlling body weight regulation.

Some aspects of this work require improving. A general remark is that, although the technical approach is sound and methodologically diverse, some of the experimental procedures requires more details and information. The sex of the mice used in the experiments, which is a critical factor particularly in studies addressing body weight regulation, was not specified in the text. The number of biological replicates is inconsistently reported, as is noted in some figures but absent in others, making it difficult to assess the robustness of the findings. Additionally, the statistical tests used are often not specified, which limits the reader’s ability to evaluate the validity of the comparisons presented. Some procedural details are lacking, at least in the main text, including the concentration and duration of several treatments (e.g., the butyrate concentration is reported in the main text for experiments in Fig. 2a and 5b, but not for most other experiments). Although some of these information is included in the material and methods, I recommend that the authors add these details to the main text, as it would help the reader not only to interpret the findings promptly but also to relate to the dosages reported in the discussion when discussing similar works in the field. I provide a more detailed list of comments below:

LINES 74-76: “The dose was selected to enhance histone acetylation without inducing adverse neurological effects, such as seizures, sluggishness, or eating ability39,40”
The information regarding the sex of the mice and the concentration of the drugs is missing. Granted that the authors refer to 2 prior publications, this information should be readily apparent, as it is very important for data interpretation.

LINES 77-78: “Notably, ICV butyrate treatment protected mice from high-fat diet (HFD)-induced weight gain and white adipose tissue (WAT) hypertrophy 78 (Fig. 1a, b).”
Mice have multiple white adipose tissue (WAT) depots, each with distinct anatomical, molecular, and physiological characteristics. It is important to specify which depot(s) were analyzed in this study and to justify the choice. This information should be made readily apparent to the reader, preferably in the main text and figure, to aid in the interpretation of the findings (same applies to Fig. 2h).

about Figure 1:
-What is the rationale for showing adipocyte area (e.g., Fig. 1b) in AU rather than in µm2?
-Fig. 1g-l: I understand that this is a cohort of mice tested in metabolic cages. Why does panel g (FI) have n =6 mice per group, but panels i-l have only 3 mice? It is not ideal to compare food intake measurements (n = 6) to metabolic readouts that depend on food intake (n = 3). Why were the other 3 mice excluded? Three mice in Fig. 1g have caloric intake similar to the average of the controls, whereas another 3 mice have a lower caloric intake. Are these 3 mice with less FI the ones excluded from panel i-g? If so, that could change the results and interpretation. Moreover, I feel that n=3 for metabolic studies is too few replicates to reach firm conclusions, and the number of replicates should be increased. Finally, are these mice males or females?

LINE 108-109: “We first treated butyrate and examined expression of several transcriptional regulators involved in ciliogenesis. “
-How long did the treatment last and what concentration of butyrate was used?

LINES 115-116: “Furthermore, direct intracerebroventricular (ICV) injection of butyrate into the 3V significantly enhanced histone acetylation and notably elongated primary cilia in h including arcuate (ARC) and VMH (Fig. 2e, f).”
-The number of mice used is not specified in the main text, figures, or figure legends. Additionally, the type of statistical test used is not reported. In Figure 2f, it appears that the statistical analysis was performed on the number of neurons, rather than on the average per mouse. Without information on the number of cilia analyzed per mouse, a subset of cells from the same mice may drive the observed differences. The authors should present the data as average cilia length per mouse, rather than as measurements from individual cilia, to ensure appropriate statistical interpretation at the animal level.

LINES 121-122: “alterations in primary cilia function within the hypothalamus. To investigate this, mice fed a HFD received butyrate either orally or via intraperitoneal injection”
These experiments differ from the ones before because butyrate is administered systemically, rather than directly in the brain. I assume that the route of administration significantly impacts the action of this molecule. The authors should provide the following information, relative to these experiments:
-Mice received butyrate via two different means, orally or via intraperitoneal injection. Why 2 different means of administration? Are controls and experimental mice treated the same way (i.e. they both received butyrate via the same route)?
-How long did the treatment last, and what concentration of butyrate was used?

LINE 125: The term “increased ciliogenesis” suggests an increase in the number or proportion of cilia; however, in the figures cited, the authors quantify cilia length. While neurons generally possess a single cilium, the use of this term may be misleading to non-experts, as it could suggest an increase in cilia number rather than in their length, as reported in the manuscript.

LINES 133-136: “To do this, we stereotaxically injected recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 2 (AAV2) either with or without the Cre recombinase fused to green fluorescent protein (AAV2-GFP as control or AAV2-Cre-GFP) into the hypothalamic 3V of mice carrying floxed alleles for both intraflagellar transport 88 and ROSA26-tdTomato (IFT88F/F::td-TomatoF/+) 37 (Fig. 3a).”
-The main text does not explicitly mention that these mice were treated with vehicle or butyrate, which should be stated. If the primary goal of these experiments (as I understand them) was to demonstrate that injection of AAV-Cre-GFP removes the cilia, wouldn’t it be sufficient to show this effect in vehicle-treated animals only? Importantly, what is concentration of butyrate, and how is it administered in this context? Systemically, as in the previous figure, or directly to the brain, similarly for data in Figs.. 1 and 3?
